title: Clast shape-fabric analysis methodology for particle-orientation in volcaniclastic deposits
author: Rodríguez-Sedano, Sarocchi, et al.

steps.title: Create binary segmented images
steps.instruction: Convert each photograph of the volcaniclastic particles into a binary image where the particles are filled white and the invisible matrix is black.

steps.title: Install and launch FabricS software
steps.instruction: Download the free FabricS program (MATLAB‑based, Windows 7 or higher) and start it on a compatible computer.

steps.title: Import segmented images
steps.instruction: In FabricS’s File section, load the binary image(s); you may import a single image or a whole set of images.

steps.title: Adjust particle‑size parameters
steps.instruction: In the Process section, set the minimum particle size and the elongation threshold that define which particles will be included in the analysis.

steps.title: Run shape‑fabric analysis
steps.instruction: Press the Fabric button to compute particle orientation, iso‑orientation degree, P‑value and generate rose diagrams; FabricS automatically applies circular‑statistics (e.g., Rayleigh test).

steps.title: Export analysis results
steps.instruction: Use the Export section to save the orientation data, statistical values and rose diagrams to files for further interpretation.

description: In order to accurately measure the shape-fabric of a sample from a volcanoclastic deposit, and obtain reliable and reproducible data, it is necessary to follow a specific procedure (Fig. 2).Fig. 2Flowchart indicating the complete protocol to effectively perform the shape fabric analysis.Fig 2 The versatility and potential of the shape-fabric analysis can be demonstrated on a study carried out in Joya Honda Maar (work in progress) located 40 km north of the city of San Luis Potosí in central Mexico. According to previous work, the eruption that created the Joya Honda maar occurred approximately 311 ± 19 ka ago along a fissure and formed a crater 1.3 × 0.9 km and 270 m deep [28]. Five eruptive phases were documented on Saucedo et al. [28], and the emission center was estimated based only by means of stratigraphy. In order to locate the possible center or centers of emission, 77 oriented samples were taken around the crater in the work of Cerca-Ruiz [27] and in Cerca-Ruiz (work in progress) (Fig. 6). All five units were sampled. However, for practical purposes and to expose the effectiveness of the method, only the results obtained from the Unit III are presented below. The complete research work will be presented later in a scientific article.Fig. 6Map of trajectories of the eruptive phases of the Joya Honda. (A) General distribution of the phases. (B) Trajectory map of UI. (C) Trajectory map of unit III. (D) Trajectory map of unit IV. (E) Trajectory map of the UV.Fig 6 A total of 38 oriented samples were collected from Unit III following the methodology described in this work. At the same time, a geophysical study (magnetometry) were performed in the maar crater and the surroundings and a ballistic impact study were carried out in the same Unit III. As a result of the shape-fabric study, a trajectory map was constructed (Fig. 6a) evidencing a possible emission zone in the northern sector of the crater.
